title: Free content
description: Free licensed works in any field
wiki_lead:
Free content, libre content, or open content (also called free information, libre information, open information) is any kind of creative work, such as a work of art, a book, a software program, or any other creative content for which copyright and other legal limitations on usage, modification and distribution are minimal. These are works or expressions which can be freely studied, applied, copied and modified by anyone for any purpose. Often this includes commercial purposes, as explicitly required by some definitions of free content. Free content encompasses all works in the public domain, as well as works copyrighted under licenses that comply with the Definition of Free Cultural Works.
In most countries, the Berne Convention grants copyright holders control over their creations by default. Therefore, copyrighted content must be explicitly declared free by the authors, which is usually accomplished by referencing or including licensing statements from within the work. The right to reuse such a work is granted by the authors in a license known as a free license, a free distribution license, or an open license, depending on the rights assigned. These freedoms given to users in the reuse of works (that is, the right to freely use, study, modify or distribute these works, possibly also for commercial purposes) are often associated with obligations (to cite the original author, to maintain the original license of the reused content) or restrictions (excluding commercial use, banning certain media) chosen by the author. There are a number of standardized licenses offering varied options that allow authors to choose the type of reuse of their work that they wish to authorize or forbid.

Definition
There are a number of different definitions of free content in regular use. Legally, however, free content is very similar to open content. An analogy is a use of the rival terms free software and open-source software, which describe ideological differences rather than legal ones. The term Open Source, by contrast, sought to encompass them all in one movement. For instance, the Open Knowledge Foundation's Open Definition describes "open" as synonymous with the definition of free in the "Definition of Free Cultural Works" (as also in the Open Source Definition and Free Software Definition). For such free/open content both movements recommend the same three Creative Commons licenses, the CC BY, CC BY-SA, and CC0.


Legal background


Copyright

Copyright is a legal concept, which gives the author or creator of a work legal control over the duplication and public performance of their work. In many jurisdictions, this is limited by a time period after which the works then enter the public domain. Copyright laws are a balance between the rights of creators of intellectual and artistic works and the rights of others to build upon those works. grok_lead: Free content is a work that anyone may use, study, copy, modify and redistribute for any purpose. The Definition of Free Cultural Works, whose stable text is version 1.1, defines free cultural works as works or expressions that can be freely studied, applied, copied and modified by anyone, for any purpose, and it names "free content" as an equivalent label. The text is not a license; it is a test of whether a work, or a free license offered for it, should be called free. If a creator takes no legal step, ordinary copyright leaves everyone else with only narrow exceptions. A work is free when a qualifying license covers it, or when its legal status â including the public domain â already supplies the same freedoms. A free license must grant four freedoms without limitation: to use and perform the work, in private or in public and for any purpose; to study it and apply what is learned from it; to redistribute copies, including by selling them, with no cap on quantity, recipient or place; and to distribute modified versions. Requirements to credit authors, and copyleft rules that keep derivative works under free terms, count as permissible restrictions, as do clauses written to protect the freedoms themselves. A license is not sufficient by itself. The material needed to make changes, such as a musical score, scientific data or source files, should be available on the same terms; a copy in a free format must exist; and technical locks, patents, contracts or similar barriers must not take the freedoms away. The pattern comes from free software. The Free Software Foundation treats "free" as liberty rather than price â free as in "free speech," not as in "free beer" â and sometimes uses the word libre so that the freedom is not confused with a zero price, while still allowing copies to be sold. Creative Commons uses the cultural-works definition to sort its own tools: works under its Attribution and Attribution-ShareAlike licenses, and public-domain material marked with CC0 or the Public Domain Mark, are labeled "Approved for Free Cultural Works." Its NonCommercial and NoDerivatives licenses are not, because they forbid some purposes or forbid adaptation. Version 2.1 of the Open Definition, written for open data, open content and open knowledge, calls that sense of "open" synonymous with "free" or "libre" in the free-software definition and the Definition of Free Cultural Works. Erik MÃ¶ller began the cultural definition to resolve ambiguous use of "free content" around Wikimedia projects, taking the free-software definition as a model; Richard Stallman, Lawrence Lessig and Angela Beesley commented during the first drafting, Benjamin Mako Hill joined as a co-initiator, and an open editing phase was announced on 1 May 2006. Lessig, Eric Eldred and Hal Abelson founded Creative Commons after Eldred v. Ashcroft, the challenge to a United States copyright-term extension, and the organization published its licenses in 2002. Wikipedia, which had used the GNU Free Documentation License as its primary text license, changed the English Wikipedia's site footer and related notices on 15 June 2009 to Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike after a community decision, and the Wikimedia Foundation standardized that wording across its projects on 30 June 2009. The change rested on version 1.3 of the Free Documentation License, which the Free Software Foundation released in November 2008 so that large collaborative sites could move to Attribution-ShareAlike. Related fields use neighboring tests. The Budapest Open Access Initiative of 14 February 2002 describes open access to scholarship as free availability on the public internet, including the right to read, copy and distribute, with attribution and the author's control over the integrity of the work as the stated limits. UNESCO's Recommendation on Open educational resources, adopted at the General Conference in Paris in November 2019, defines those resources as public-domain or openly licensed teaching, learning and research materials that permit no-cost access, reuse, adaptation and redistribution.
